method.deep_poverty: Share of people with equivalised AHC income below 40% and 50% of the person-weighted median AHC income in the same year

comparators.child_poverty: DWP, Low income poverty projections for children, FYE 2026 to FYE 2031 (July 2026)

notes: Model figures are unvalidated demo output from the Microcosm dataset.
Income outturn is HBAI, published in real terms; BHC cash values are recovered with OBR CPI, and AHC outturn is shown in real terms only.
Poverty and inequality outturn is the HBAI admin-linked series, which starts in 2021-22.
The 2024-25 model point uses the weights solved for 2025, scaled for population, so it carries 2025 composition and caseloads (UC £74bn).
OBR series are calendar years; CPI after housing costs and social rent are PolicyEngine derivations, not OBR forecasts.
The Autumn Budget 2026 OBR forecast is due on 28 October 2026; until then the post-Budget series repeat the pre-Budget ones.
caveats: Ages and benefit take-up are held fixed, so the State Pension age rise to 67 removes State Pension from 66-year-olds with no work response.
The population is uprated uniformly, so its age structure stays as in 2025.
Results for small groups are noisy: calibration roughly halves the effective sample, so family-size and two-child figures are approximate.
The September 2026 free school meals expansion to all Universal Credit families in England is not modelled, so child poverty from 2026-27 is a little high.
The Universal Credit health element is assigned too widely (through disabled children, and twice to some couples), so child poverty is a little low.
The above-inflation rises in the Universal Credit standard allowance from 2027-28 are missing, so UC is about £0.6bn too low by 2029-30.

notes: The absolute line is the official one: 60% of the 2024-25 HBAI median (£431.69 a week before housing costs for a couple), uprated by CPI. Our 2024-25 incomes are higher than in HBAI at the bottom and middle of the distribution (median about 6% higher), so absolute and relative poverty both sit below official figures. On the same survey records with the survey's own weights the model reproduces the HBAI median and poverty rates; the difference comes from reweighting the data to 2025 administrative totals. Read the projections as changes from 2024-25.

notes: Deciles are re-ranked each year, so growth compares the same position in the distribution, not the same people.

The lowest tenth's real median after housing costs falls 5% to 2029-30, while the other tenths move within about 0.6%. That median is the 5th percentile, a noisy point, and the fall sits in the bottom 5%. The largest driver is the State Pension age rise to 67 on a dataset whose ages are held fixed; next is Local Housing Allowance frozen beyond 2026-27, an assumption rather than law.
The halves are split at the non-pensioner median and show means, not the typical (median) incomes in Resolution Foundation analysis.

groups.three_plus_children: Three or more children in family

notes: Relative child poverty after housing costs falls 1.6 points in 2026-27, from 26.8% to 25.3%. DWP's July 2026 projections, on the same OBR forecast and the new HBAI series, fall about 3 points (28% to 25%).

Removing the two-child limit lowers child poverty by 2.0 points (about 290,000 children) in 2026-27, close to DWP's estimate of 2.2 points (300,000). By 2029-30 the effect is 3.0 points (440,000), against DWP's 3.2 points (450,000).

Our net fall is smaller mainly because, with the limit removed, our child poverty is otherwise flat between 2025-26 and 2026-27, while DWP's central figures imply other changes lower it. Part of that is the September 2026 free school meals expansion, which our baseline leaves out and DWP puts at 0.4 points in 2026-27. DWP's figures are rounded, and the difference is within our sampling uncertainty.

The 2025-26 counts of affected families match DWP's statistics because the data are calibrated to them. In 2026-27, 64% of children in affected families are in relative poverty after housing costs with the limit kept, and 49% after its removal.
sources: DWP, Low income poverty projections for children, FYE 2026 to FYE 2031 (July 2026)

DWP, Universal Credit claimants: statistics on the two child limit policy
DWP, Child Poverty Strategy: impact on low income poverty levels (December 2025)

notes: Outturn is HBAI Table 1.2b: Gini, and the ratio of top to bottom quintile medians, which is the 90th over the 10th percentile.

Read the projection as a change, not a level. Our Gini is about 2.5 points below official figures in 2024-25 before housing costs (3.0 after). Our data have fewer very low incomes, and we treat very high incomes differently from the SPI-based adjustment in HBAI. The 90:10 ratio is low (3.35 against 3.71 before housing costs, 4.04 against 4.54 after) because the bottom tenth is too high, not because the top is too low.
